questions.title: Async & Promises practice 1
questions.prompt: What does an async function always return?
choices: A Promise
A timer id
A callback
Only undefined
questions.explanation: JavaScript wraps a returned value in a fulfilled Promise, or returns a rejected Promise when the function throws.

questions.title: Async & Promises practice 2
questions.prompt: What happens when an awaited Promise rejects?
choices: An error is thrown at the await expression
The browser closes
Await returns null automatically
The function restarts
questions.explanation: Rejection enters the surrounding catch just like a synchronous throw, or rejects the async function when it is not caught.

questions.title: Trace Async & Promises
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The function waits for loadUser to settle, then prints either the returned name or a controlled failure message. The resulting output is 'Depends on the request result.'.

questions.title: Async & Promises practice 5
questions.prompt: In `const user = fetch("/api/user"); console.log(user.name);`, why is `user.name` undefined?
choices: fetch returns a Promise, not the user, so name must be awaited first
fetch always fails on a relative URL
console.log cannot print object properties
name is a reserved word in JavaScript
questions.explanation: `fetch` hands back a Promise immediately, before the response exists, so `user` is that Promise and `user.name` is undefined. You must `await` the fetch and then `await response.json()` to reach the real object. The correct version does both. Nothing here is about reserved words or console.log's abilities.

questions.title: Fetch status checks
questions.prompt: After `fetch` returns a response, what status check should code usually make?
choices: Check `response.ok` before treating the response as successful data.
Treat a fulfilled fetch response as successful without checking its HTTP status.
Check only whether the response variable exists.
Parse JSON first and decide whether the status mattered later.
questions.explanation: `fetch` rejects for network-level failures, but an HTTP 404 or 500 can still produce a fulfilled response object. Checking `response.ok` keeps failed responses from being parsed and displayed as if they were successful data.

questions.title: Await needed values
choices: Run independent requests one after another without a reason.
Await the operation that produces the needed value.
Use a Promise value before it has settled.
Catch an error and return data shaped like success.
questions.explanation: Use `await` when later code needs the value produced by an asynchronous operation. It pauses the current async function until that operation settles; it does not freeze the whole browser or finish unrelated promises automatically.

questions.title: HTTP success
questions.prompt: Why check HTTP response status before parsing JSON?
choices: A failed HTTP status may not contain the successful data shape the code expects.
JSON parsing automatically changes 404 responses into successful data.
The status check makes the network request finish faster.
The status check replaces the need for await.
questions.explanation: A failed HTTP status may come with an error page or error payload instead of the data shape your code expects. Checking status first lets the code route failure to an error path before parsing and rendering.

questions.title: Async recovery
questions.prompt: Where should async failures be caught?
choices: Start async work but never return or await it.
Assume `await` freezes the whole browser.
Handle all failures with an empty catch.
Catch failures where recovery is possible.
questions.explanation: Catch failures where the code can recover or communicate clearly, such as showing a retry option or fallback. Empty catches make async bugs feel like nothing happened, which is frustrating for users and developers.

questions.title: Concurrent requests
questions.prompt: When can independent async requests run concurrently?
choices: Keep independent requests concurrent when appropriate.
Use `Promise.all` when one optional request may fail independently.
Forget that an async function always returns a Promise.
Create race conditions by updating stale state.
questions.explanation: If two requests do not need each other's results, starting them together can avoid unnecessary waiting. If one can fail independently, choose a pattern that handles that failure intentionally instead of collapsing unrelated work.

questions.title: Promise timing
choices: Retry requests forever without a limit.
Work with values that become available after the current code finishes.
Ignore cancellation when a screen changes.
Treat pending data as if it already exists.
questions.explanation: A Promise represents work whose value may become available later. Code should treat pending data as not ready yet, then handle success or failure when the Promise settles.
